openingProblem.problem: In June 1948 Stalin cut off West Berlin by land and water from the West. Eleven months later he lifted the blockade having gained nothing. Why did the first great crisis of the Cold War end without a shot being fired?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: why did Stalin back down?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Why Berlin? The causes of the blockade
chunks.body:
Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone of Germany, but it was itself divided into four sectors. The Western powers held the western sectors; the only written agreement on access to the city covered air corridors. When the wartime alliance broke down, the question was whether West Berlin would remain in Western hands or be absorbed into Soviet-controlled eastern Germany.

The crisis grew from the division of Germany. On 1 January 1947 the US and Britain merged their zones into "Bizonia". In March 1947 a foreign ministers' conference in Moscow broke down and Truman announced his doctrine; in June the Marshall Plan offered aid that would, in the Office of the Historian's words, "create a bulwark against Communism" by drawing Western Europe into the American economic orbit. The Prague coup of February 1948 convinced the West that Stalin had chosen confrontation, and in March Britain, France and the Benelux states formed the Brussels Pact.

In early 1948 the Western powers met in London and agreed to extend the Marshall Plan to western Germany and to plan a West German government, which Judt calls an explicit departure from the spirit of the Potsdam agreements. When the Soviets learned of the plans, their representative, Marshal Sokolovsky, walked out of the Allied Control Council on 20 March. From 1 April Soviet authorities began to interfere with traffic to Berlin. "The real Cold War in Europe," Judt writes, "had begun."

The trigger was money. On 18 June 1948 the Western powers announced a new currency, the **Deutsche Mark**, for their zones; the notes had been printed in secret in the United States. They introduced it to West Berlin too, without informing the Soviets. The aim was to take economic control of the city from the Soviets, open it to Marshall aid and end the black market. On 23 June the Soviets issued their own East German mark and cut the rail lines to Berlin.

Stalin's aim, Judt argues, was to force the West to choose: either quit Berlin or abandon the plan for a separate West German state, which was what he really wanted to stop. Berlin was a bargaining chip.

This mattered because the blockade was a response to the creation of a Western German state, which meant that the crisis was really about the future of Germany rather than the city alone.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The division of Germany and Western plans for a West German state caused the crisis.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Soviets had also broken the Potsdam accords.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The currency reform was the immediate trigger.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Soviets had interfered with traffic since April.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin used Berlin as a bargaining chip over Germany.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The West could not know his limited aims at the time.

chunks.title: Blockade and airlift, June 1948–May 1949
chunks.body:
From 24 June 1948 West Berlin was cut off by land and water. West Berliners, in a city still in ruins, depended on supplies from outside. The Western powers had few military options, because the Red Army around Berlin dwarfed their own forces. On 13 June General Lucius Clay, the American commander in Germany, had cabled Washington that staying in Berlin was "essential to our prestige in Germany and in Europe... it has become a symbol of the American intent". The Truman administration agreed.

The answer was an **airlift**. The written agreements of 1945 guaranteed the Western Allies air corridors to Berlin. If the Soviets attacked unarmed transport planes, the onus of starting a war would be theirs. The first American plane landed at Tempelhof on 26 June ("Operation Vittles"), and the British followed two days later ("Operation Plainfare"). Judt credits the British Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, with persuading the Americans to lead the airlift. At the same time Truman sent B-29 bombers capable of carrying nuclear weapons to Britain, a signal that the US was able and willing to use force.

The first months were difficult, and Berlin's politics became tense. The Soviets offered to lift the blockade if the West withdrew the Deutschmark from West Berlin; the Allies refused. In September 1948 the East German Communist party, the SED, forced the city council to adjourn. In response, 300,000 West Berliners gathered at the Reichstag to oppose Soviet domination, and the turnout convinced the Western powers to keep both the airlift and the new currency.

The airlift grew steadily more efficient. At its height a plane landed at Tempelhof every 45 seconds. Over eleven months the Western allies flew in some 2.3 million tons of food on 277,500 flights; 73 Allied airmen died. By spring 1949 it was clear that the airlift could go on indefinitely. Meanwhile a Western counter-blockade caused severe shortages in eastern Germany.

This mattered because the airlift turned a Soviet threat into a test of Western endurance that the West could pass without firing a shot, which meant that Stalin had to choose between war and retreat.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was a huge and risky logistical gamble.

argumentsThatWork.claim: West Berliners' resistance kept the West committed.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Western powers also feared losing prestige across Europe.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The airlift proved it could be sustained indefinitely.

chunks.title: Why did Stalin fail?
chunks.body:
Stalin had two aims: to force the West out of Berlin or, more importantly, to stop the creation of a separate West German state. He achieved neither. Why?

First, the West could sustain the airlift. By spring 1949 the airlift was delivering more each month, and the Western powers had shown they could continue indefinitely. Meanwhile the Western counter-blockade was causing shortages in eastern Germany that Moscow feared might lead to unrest.

Second, Stalin would not go to war. Judt argues that, "like most of Stalin's diplomatic adventures", the blockade was "an improvisation, not part of any calculated aggressive design", although the West could not know this at the time. Shooting down the transport planes would have meant attacking an unarmed humanitarian mission, and the presence of American B-29s in Britain was a reminder of the US atomic monopoly. Judt adds that the US had only 56 atomic bombs and no settled policy on using them, and that Truman was reluctant to consider it; but the Soviets could not be sure of that.

Third, the blockade backfired politically. Coming soon after the Prague coup, it made the Western powers more determined to press ahead with West Germany, and it made division more acceptable to Germans themselves. France joined its zone to the Bizone in April 1949, creating a West German economic unit of 49 million people, against 17 million in the Soviet zone.

When the blockade failed, Stalin changed course. On 31 January 1949 he publicly offered to lift it in return for postponing the West German state. The West refused. On 12 May 1949 the Soviet Union ended the blockade in return for nothing more than a conference of foreign ministers, which met on 23 May and achieved nothing.

This mattered because the blockade was Stalin's first major defeat in the Cold War, which meant that the Western powers learned that firmness without war could work.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Stalin had not expected the West to sustain it.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It also deepened the division of Germany.

chunks.title: Consequences: two Germanies and a divided Europe
chunks.body:
The Berlin crisis reshaped Europe. Judt identifies three major outcomes.

**First, two German states.** The crisis led directly to the creation of two Germanies, an outcome none of the Allies had sought in 1945. While the foreign ministers met in vain in May and June 1949, the West German Basic Law came into effect, and on 15 September Konrad Adenauer became the first Chancellor of the Federal Republic. Stalin answered with a separate East German state, formally created on 7 October 1949. For the West a divided Germany had become an attractive outcome; for Stalin, once he could neither win over the Germans nor stop the Western plans, an East German Communist state was "the least bad outcome".

**Second, an American commitment to Europe.** The crisis committed the United States, for the first time, to a significant military presence in Europe for the indefinite future. Shortly before the blockade ended, the Western powers created **NATO**, the first peacetime alliance the US had joined outside the Western Hemisphere. The Berlin crisis was one of the events of 1947–48 that convinced Western Europeans they needed American protection, and in May 1948 the US Senate's Vandenberg Resolution had opened the way to the treaty.

**Third, a new military calculation.** If the West was going to protect West Germany, it would need the means to do so. The bombers sent to Britain in 1948 marked the beginning of a reappraisal of Western military strategy, including the role of atomic weapons.

The crisis also changed the meaning of Berlin. Once associated with Prussian militarism and Nazism, West Berlin became, in the Office of the Historian's words, "a symbol of democracy and freedom in the fight against Communism". It was one of the few places on earth where American and Soviet forces stood face to face.

This mattered because the Berlin Blockade turned the division of Germany and of Europe into a fixed military fact, which meant that the Cold War in Europe now had a front line that would last for forty years.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Brussels Pact of 1948 had already begun European defence cooperation.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the currency reform of June 1948 the main cause of the Berlin Blockade?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far

modelPlan.thesis: The currency reform was the trigger, but the underlying cause was the Western decision to build a West German state, which Stalin tried to stop by using Berlin as a bargaining chip.

arguments.claim: The currency reform as trigger (named factor first).
Western plans for a West German state.
The wider breakdown: Bizonia, Marshall, Prague.
Stalin's aims: Berlin as a bargaining chip.

modelPlan.counter: Soviet interference with traffic began on 1 April, before the currency reform, so the crisis was already under way.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Trigger or cause? The currency reform made the break visible, but the West German state was what Stalin wanted to stop.

segments.text: The currency reform was the trigger of the Berlin Blockade, but not its main cause.
The Deutsche Mark was announced on 18 June 1948 and introduced to West Berlin without informing the Soviets, who cut the rail lines on 23 June.
This meant that a separate Western economy now included West Berlin, so Stalin had to act quickly if he was to stop a West German state.
However, the London Conference had already agreed to plan a West German government, and Soviet interference with traffic began on 1 April.
The currency reform was therefore the immediate cause, while the Western plan for West Germany was the main cause.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The Berlin Blockade was a victory for the West.” Discuss with reference to the period 1948 to 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: a victory for the West
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: Berlin, Germany, or Europe?

modelPlan.thesis: The blockade was a clear Western victory, since Stalin secured neither of his aims and the West kept Berlin and created West Germany and NATO; but it also fixed the division of Germany and Europe.

arguments.claim: For: Stalin secured neither aim.
For: West Germany and NATO.
For: Berlin as a symbol of freedom.
Against: Germany divided; a new front line.

modelPlan.counter: Judt suggests division was the 'least bad outcome' for Stalin too, so both sides gained something.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By each side's aims, the West won; by the effect on Germany, both accepted division.

segments.text: The Berlin Blockade was a clear victory for the West.
Stalin ended the blockade on 12 May 1949 in return only for a conference, and that year the Federal Republic and NATO were created.
This meant that Stalin had secured neither of his aims, so the West kept Berlin and completed its plans for Germany.
However, the crisis also fixed the division of Germany, and Judt notes that an East German state was Stalin's 'least bad outcome'.
The blockade was therefore a Western victory in the crisis, though its price was a divided Germany.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the Berlin Blockade (1948–1949).

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The blockade was caused by the Western plan for a West German state, triggered by the currency reform; its main consequences were two German states, NATO and a lasting US commitment to Europe.

arguments.claim: Cause: the London plans and the ACC collapse.
Cause: the currency reform.
Consequence: two German states.
Consequence: NATO and the US commitment.

modelPlan.counter: Both sides had been moving towards division before the crisis, so it accelerated rather than caused it.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The US military presence in Europe, which outlasted the Cold War.

segments.text: The Berlin Blockade was caused by the Western decision to build a West German state.
The London Conference of 1948 planned a West German government, and the Deutsche Mark, announced on 18 June, was introduced to West Berlin without Soviet agreement.
This meant that Stalin used Berlin to force the West to choose, but the airlift defeated him, so the West German state went ahead.
However, the crisis also led to an East German state on 7 October 1949, fixing the division of Germany.
Its most significant consequence was therefore the American commitment to Europe through NATO.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons why the Berlin airlift succeeded between 1948 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh the reasons, then judge

modelPlan.thesis: The airlift succeeded because it used the one legal access route, putting the onus of war on Stalin, who would not fight; Western logistics and Berliners' resistance made it sustainable.

arguments.claim: Legal access and the onus of war.
Stalin's unwillingness to fight.
Logistics: a plane every 45 seconds.
Berliners' resistance.

modelPlan.counter: The US atomic monopoly may also have deterred the Soviets, though Judt says the US had no policy on using it.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? Stalin's refusal to go to war, without which the airlift could have been stopped.

segments.text: The airlift succeeded above all because Stalin was not prepared to go to war over Berlin.
The only written access agreements covered the air corridors, so stopping the airlift meant attacking unarmed planes, and Judt calls the blockade 'an improvisation'.
This meant that once the West flew in some 2.3 million tons, Stalin had no way to win without war, so he retreated in May 1949.
However, the airlift also depended on West Berliners' resistance, shown by the 300,000 who rallied in September 1948.
Stalin's refusal to fight was therefore the decisive reason, while logistics and popular will made the airlift sustainable.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the aims of Stalin and the Western powers in the Berlin crisis of 1948–1949.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The aims of Stalin and the West

modelPlan.thesis: Both sides wanted to avoid war and to shape Germany's future, but Stalin wanted to stop a West German state while the West wanted to build one and stay in Berlin, and only the West achieved its aims.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both wanted to avoid war.
Similarity: both saw Berlin as a symbol and a lever.
Difference: stop a West German state against build one.
Difference: outcomes.

modelPlan.counter: Judt suggests division was acceptable to both sides in the end, so their aims converged.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Over Germany: the crisis was about the West German state, not the city.

segments.text: Stalin and the Western powers both sought to shape Germany's future without war, but their aims were opposed.
Stalin used Berlin as a bargaining chip to stop a West German state, whereas the West, as Clay put it, saw Berlin as 'a symbol of the American intent' and pressed on with its plans.
This meant that the blockade was a test of will over Germany, so whoever held out would decide the outcome.
However, both sides avoided war: the West refused to use force and Stalin would not shoot down the planes.
The decisive difference was therefore over Germany, and only the West achieved its aim.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the significance of the Berlin Blockade for the Cold War in Europe between 1948 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The blockade was significant because it fixed the division of Germany, brought the US permanently into European defence through NATO, and established that the Cold War in Europe could be fought without war.

arguments.claim: Two German states.
NATO and the US commitment.
A military reappraisal.
Berlin as a symbol.

modelPlan.counter: Much of this was already under way before the blockade, for example the Brussels Pact of March 1948.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How did the outcomes connect? Two German states needed defending, which required the US commitment and NATO.

segments.text: The Berlin Blockade was significant because it turned the division of Europe into a fixed military fact.
It led to two German states in 1949 and, Judt argues, committed the US for the first time to an indefinite military presence in Europe, with NATO founded shortly before the blockade ended.
This meant that the West now had to defend West Germany, so a new military calculation, including atomic weapons, followed.
However, the Brussels Pact of March 1948 and the London plans show that division and alliance were already under way.
The blockade's significance was therefore to accelerate and lock in the Cold War's front line in Europe.
